summary: Nelson Cowan's 2008 chapter in Progress in Brain Research clarifies the distinctions among long-term, short-term, and working memory. It argues that short-term memory may differ from long-term memory in temporal decay and chunk capacity limits, both still debated but supported by recent evidence. It reviews definitions of working memory and presents a theoretical framework in which short-term memory is a temporarily activated subset of long-term memory, with a limited-capacity focus of attention. The note is cut off mid-discussion of rehearsal and chunking.
one_line: Nelson Cowan's chapter distinguishes long-term, short-term, and working memory, evaluating evidence for decay and capacity limits in short-term memory.
key_facts: The chapter is by Nelson Cowan and was published in Prog Brain Res in 2008, volume 169, pages 323–338.
Long- and short-term memory could differ in two fundamental ways, with only short-term memory demonstrating (1) temporal decay and (2) chunk capacity limits.

Working memory has been defined in three slightly discrepant ways: as short-term memory applied to cognitive tasks, as a multi-component system, and as the use of attention to manage short-term memory.
Ebbinghaus examined his own acquisition and forgetting of nonsense syllables at periods up to 31 days.
James (1890) proposed a distinction between primary memory, the small amount of information held as the trailing edge of the conscious present, and secondary memory.
McGeoch (1932) argued that forgetting over time was largely due to interference during the retention interval rather than inevitable decay.
Miller et al. (1960) used the term working memory to refer to memory as it is used to plan and carry out behavior.
Baddeley and Hitch (1974) demonstrated that a single module could not account for all kinds of temporary memory, and Baddeley (2000) added an episodic buffer to the model.
Measures of working memory correlate with intellectual aptitudes, especially fluid intelligence, better than measures of short-term memory.
Lewandowsky et al. (2004) found no evidence of memory decay across response times between 400 and 1600 ms even with articulatory suppression.

Cowan and Aubuchon (in press) found performance was better with a short first half of response intervals (M=.70) than a long first half (M=.67) when recall timing had to match presentation timing, suggesting decay.
Peterson and Peterson (1959) found severe memory loss for letter trigrams as the filled delay increased up to 18 s, which sceptics attributed to temporal distinctiveness and proactive interference.
Baddeley and Scott (1971) found an effect of test delay within the first 5 s but not at longer delays.
Miller (1956) discussed the 'magical number seven plus or minus two', but Miller's autobiographical essay (1989) indicates he was never very serious about the number seven.
Later studies suggested the capacity limit is typically three or four units (Broadbent, 1975; Cowan, 2001).
Individual working memory capacity in adults ranges from about two to six items, and is a strong correlate of cognitive aptitude.
